Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider a decoupled linear system of ODEs
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = λ_{1}x(t); y^{′}(t) = λ_{2}y(t)]

Content:
Recall that the eigenvalues for a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2.]
The corresponding eigenvectors are parallel to the coordinate axes:
[MATH: [1; 0]]
So, the general solution of the system is given by
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
Notice that if a solution starts on one of the coordinate axes, it remains on that axis. These are called straight-line solutions:

Content:
- On the [MATH: x]-axis ([MATH: c_2=0]):
[MATH: [1; 0]]
- On the [MATH: y]-axis ([MATH: c_1=0]):
[MATH: [0; 1]]

Content:
The stability of these solutions as [MATH: t\to\infty] depends on the signs of the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2.] We will explore the three main stability cases in the upcoming examples.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: One Positive and One Negative Eigenvalue

Content:
Suppose we have a decoupled system
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = λ_{1}x(t); y^{′}(t) = λ_{2}y(t)]
where [MATH: \lambda_1>0] and [MATH: \lambda_2<0] (the opposite case, where [MATH: \lambda_1<0] and [MATH: \lambda_2>0,] is similar).

Content:
Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

Content:
- The straight-line solutions on the [MATH: x]-axis have the form [MATH: [1; 0]] Since [MATH: \lambda_1>0,] we have that [MATH: e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] Thus, the trajectories on the [MATH: x]-axis move away from the origin. This is called an unstable axis.
- The straight-line solutions on the [MATH: y]-axis have the form [MATH: [0; 1]] Since [MATH: \lambda_2<0,] we have that [MATH: e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] Thus, the trajectories on the [MATH: y]-axis move toward the origin. This is called a stable axis.

Content:
Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a saddle point.

Content:
In the phase portrait, we draw

Content:
- arrows on the [MATH: x]-axis pointing outward (away from the origin), while
- arrows on the [MATH: y]-axis pointing inward (toward the origin).

Content:
A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8c408e75330110a0b57de1d2f9b585d5]

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Both Positive Eigenvalues

Content:
Suppose we have a decoupled system
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = λ_{1}x(t); y^{′}(t) = λ_{2}y(t)]
where [MATH: \lambda_1,\lambda_2>0.]

Content:
Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

Content:
- The straight-line solutions on the [MATH: x]-axis have the form [MATH: [1; 0]] Since [MATH: \lambda_1>0,] we have that [MATH: e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] Thus, the trajectories on the [MATH: x]-axis move away from the origin (unstable axis).
- The straight-line solutions on the [MATH: y]-axis have the form [MATH: [0; 1]] Since [MATH: \lambda_2>0,] we have that [MATH: e^{\lambda_2 t} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] Thus, the trajectories on the [MATH: y]-axis move away from the origin (unstable axis).

Content:
Because both axes are unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called an unstable node or source.

Content:
In the phase portrait, we draw:

Content:
- arrows on the [MATH: x]-axis pointing outward (away from the origin), and
- arrows on the [MATH: y]-axis pointing outward (away from the origin).

Content:
A typical trajectory for an unstable node emanates from the origin toward infinity.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c6bb75a13c9205e480c13924447b4674]

---

Item 4 — Tutorial: Both Negative Eigenvalues

Content:
Suppose we have a decoupled system
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = λ_{1}x(t); y^{′}(t) = λ_{2}y(t)]
where [MATH: \lambda_1,\lambda_2<0.]

Content:
Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

Content:
- The straight-line solutions on the [MATH: x]-axis have the form [MATH: [1; 0]] Since [MATH: \lambda_1<0,] we have that [MATH: e^{\lambda_1 t} \to 0] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] Thus, the trajectories on the [MATH: x]-axis move toward the origin (stable axis).
- The straight-line solutions on the [MATH: y]-axis have the form [MATH: [0; 1]] Since [MATH: \lambda_2<0,] we have that [MATH: e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] Thus, the trajectories on the [MATH: y]-axis move toward the origin (stable axis).

Content:
Because both axes are stable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a stable node or sink.

Content:
In the phase portrait, we draw

Content:
- arrows on the [MATH: x]-axis pointing inward (toward the origin), and
- arrows on the [MATH: y]-axis pointing inward (toward the origin).

Content:
A typical trajectory flows into the origin.

[IMG: /graphics/bfb450e939b790c3e7baec3711f296c8]

[MATH: [0; 1]]

Item 11 — Tutorial: Dominant Eigenvalue

Content:
For a decoupled system
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = λ_{1}x(t); y^{′}(t) = λ_{2}y(t)]
we know the signs of [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] tell us the type of the equilibrium (sink/source/saddle). But how can we determine the shape of trajectories in cases when the origin is a source ([MATH: \lambda_1,\lambda_2 > 0]) or a sink ([MATH: \lambda_1,\lambda_2 < 0])?

Content:
To do this, we can compare the rates of change of [MATH: x(t)] and [MATH: y(t)] by looking at the slope of the tangent line to the trajectory, [MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.] Assuming [MATH: c_1,c_2\neq 0,] we have:
[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}
=
\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}
=
\frac{\lambda_2 y(t)}{\lambda_1 x(t)}
=
\frac{\lambda_2 c_2}{\lambda_1 c_1}\,e^{(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)t}.]
As we can see, the long-term behavior of the slope as [MATH: t \to \infty] depends on the sign of the exponent, [MATH: \lambda_2-\lambda_1.]

Content:
This comparison is governed by which eigenvalue has the larger magnitude. We call the eigenvalue with the largest absolute value the dominant eigenvalue.

Content:
In the next slides, we will analyze the source and sink cases separately.

---

Item 12 — Tutorial: Unstable Node (Source)

Content:
Let's analyze the case where the origin is a source, with [MATH: 0 < \lambda_1, \lambda_2.] Recall that for a source, trajectories approach infinity as [MATH: t \to \infty.]

Content:
- If [MATH: 0<\lambda_2<\lambda_1,] then [MATH: \lambda_1] is the dominant eigenvalue and [MATH: \lambda_2-\lambda_1<0.] In this case:
[MATH: e^{(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)t} \to 0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \to 0]
as [MATH: t\to\infty.] This means the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories move away from the origin.
- If [MATH: 0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2,] then [MATH: \lambda_2] is the dominant eigenvalue and [MATH: \lambda_2-\lambda_1>0.] In this case:
[MATH: e^{(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)t} \to \infty
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \to \infty]
as [MATH: t\to\infty.] This means the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as the trajectories move away from the origin.

Content:
Notice that in both cases, trajectories become parallel to the axis corresponding to the dominant eigenvalue as they move away from the origin (the [MATH: x]-axis on the left, and the [MATH: y]-axis on the right).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fed5af1f8d54f5dcb2b163fa60f29469]

---

Item 13 — Tutorial: Stable Node (Sink)

Content:
Now, let's analyze the case where the origin is a sink, with [MATH: \lambda_1, \lambda_2 < 0.] For a sink, trajectories approach the origin as [MATH: t \to \infty.]

Content:
- If [MATH: \lambda_2<\lambda_1<0,] then [MATH: \lambda_2] is the dominant eigenvalue and [MATH: \lambda_2-\lambda_1<0.] As [MATH: t\to\infty:]
[MATH: e^{(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)t} \to 0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \to 0]
This means the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as trajectories approach the origin.
- If [MATH: \lambda_1<\lambda_2<0,] then [MATH: \lambda_1] is the dominant eigenvalue and [MATH: \lambda_2-\lambda_1>0.] As [MATH: t\to\infty:]
[MATH: e^{(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)t} \to \infty
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \to \infty]
This means the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as trajectories approach the origin.

Content:
Notice that in both cases, trajectories become parallel to the axis corresponding to the eigenvalue closest to zero (not the dominant one) as they move toward the origin (the [MATH: x]-axis on the left, and the [MATH: y]-axis on the right).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0bfe8aa6ee3637e430d44dafaf5e0a22]

---

- Eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_2=-4] with the corresponding eigenvector [MATH: [0; 1]]

The general solution of the system is
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
[MATH: [1; 0]]
lie on the [MATH: x]-axis. Since [MATH: e^{-t} \to 0] as [MATH: t \to \infty,] these solutions approach the origin as [MATH: t \to \infty.]
- The straight-line solutions of the form
[MATH: [0; 1]]
lie on the [MATH: y]-axis. Since [MATH: e^{-4t} \to 0] as [MATH: t \to \infty,] these solutions also approach the origin as [MATH: t \to \infty.]

Item 17 — Tutorial: Classification of Equilibria

Content:
Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Content:
Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = λ_{1}x(t); y^{′}(t) = λ_{2}y(t)]

Content:
Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin [MATH: (0,0).]
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2.]

Content:
First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

Content:
- On the [MATH: x]-axis, we have [MATH: y(t)= 0] and [MATH: x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}].

- If [MATH: \lambda_1<0,] the [MATH: x]-axis is a stable line.
- If [MATH: \lambda_1>0,] the [MATH: x]-axis is an unstable line.
- On the [MATH: y]-axis, we have [MATH: x(t)=0] and [MATH: y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.]

- If [MATH: \lambda_2<0,] the [MATH: y]-axis is a stable line.
- If [MATH: \lambda_2>0,] the [MATH: y]-axis is an unstable line.

Content:
As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

Content:
- Unstable node (source) if [MATH: \lambda_1>0] and [MATH: \lambda_2>0.]
- Stable node (sink) if [MATH: \lambda_1<0] and [MATH: \lambda_2<0.] In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.
- Saddle point if [MATH: \lambda_1\lambda_2<0] (one positive, one negative).
